open: Determine the composition-dependent boundary between mono-oxo and non-oxo Pa(V) complexes in mixed chloride/fluoride and other competing acidic media. Measure species fractions across that boundary.
status: A 2026 study established a roughly 1.83 Å Pa–O bond persisting even in highly acidic chloride solution. Its persistence with competing ligands remains unresolved; acidity alone does not provide the missing speciation rule.
why: Makes protactinium chemistry predictable across changes of medium.
key_works: M. Maloubier et al. (2026; online 2025), “Persistent Mono-Oxo Bonding with Protactinium(V) Revealed in Highly Acidic Chloride Solutions,” [DOI: 10.1002/anie.202518403](https://doi.org/10.1002/anie.202518403).

title: Resolving inverse trans influence in a Pa(V) solution complex
open: Experimentally distinguish trans and cis Pa–Cl distances in the mono-oxo chloride complex. Test the predicted inverse trans influence independently of fitting a calculated geometry.
status: The 2026 analysis predicts trans-bond shortening of 0.04–0.08 Å. That difference falls within the EXAFS uncertainty and was not resolved experimentally.
why: Tests a directional-bonding prediction for an exceptionally data-poor actinide.
key_works: M. Maloubier et al. (2026; online 2025), “Persistent Mono-Oxo Bonding with Protactinium(V) Revealed in Highly Acidic Chloride Solutions,” [DOI: 10.1002/anie.202518403](https://doi.org/10.1002/anie.202518403).

title: Isolation of a molecular promethium(II) complex
open: Isolate a molecular Pm(II) complex and establish metal-centered reduction and coordination geometry independently of ligand-radical alternatives.
status: Anderson-Sanchez’s 2024 dissertation identifies Pm as the missing radioactive member of the molecular divalent-lanthanide series. The 2024 aqueous Pm–diglycolamide structure establishes Pm(III), leaving divalent isolation as a distinct target.
why: Supplies a missing test of how configuration and ligand symmetry control lanthanide reduction.
key_works: L. M. Anderson-Sanchez (2024), “Understanding the Role of Steric Factors in the Successful Isolation of Low Oxidation State Lanthanide and Actinide Complexes,” [doctoral dissertation](https://escholarship.org/uc/item/0nz1t51t); D. M. Driscoll et al. (2024), “Observation of a promethium complex in solution,” [DOI: 10.1038/s41586-024-07267-6](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-024-07267-6).

title: Site-resolved explanation of flerovium’s two adsorption populations
open: Quantify contributions from weak terrace adsorption, surface diffusion, and trapping at rare active gold sites to flerovium deposition. Use characterized surfaces and independently testable kinetic predictions.
status: A 2022 study reconciled contrasting adsorption observations using inhomogeneous surfaces and a proposed two-stage mechanism. Experimental discrimination of the individual adsorption states remains the narrower unresolved target.
why: Separates intrinsic element reactivity from the microscopic structure of the detector.
key_works: A. Yakushev et al. (2022), “On the adsorption and reactivity of element 114, flerovium,” [DOI: 10.3389/fchem.2022.976635](https://doi.org/10.3389/fchem.2022.976635).

title: Direct chemical-form verification of chromatographed nihonium and moscovium
open: Determine directly whether transported and adsorbed Nh/Mc species are atoms, ions, or trace-impurity compounds. Link molecular identity to the measured chromatogram.
status: The 2024 experiment measured adsorption-enthalpy magnitudes near 58 and 54 kJ/mol and supported atomic assignments computationally. Direct mass-sensitive identification, developed for other heavy elements in 2025, remains a stronger proposed test.
why: Makes apparent relativistic reactivity trends independent of assumed chemical identity.
key_works: A. Yakushev et al. (2024), “Manifestation of relativistic effects in the chemical properties of nihonium and moscovium revealed by gas chromatography studies,” [DOI: 10.3389/fchem.2024.1474820](https://doi.org/10.3389/fchem.2024.1474820); F. H. Garcia et al. (2025), “Atom-at-a-Time Radioactive Molecule Identification: Looking toward Studies of Superheavy Elements,” [DOI: 10.1021/acs.jpca.5c02098](https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.jpca.5c02098).

title: Does oxygen-bound seaborgium hexaisocarbonyl exist as a metastable molecule?
open: Establish whether Sg(OC)₆ is a genuine metastable minimum after correlation, spin–orbit, and vibrational effects are included. Determine its isomerization lifetime and a distinguishing experimental signature if it is viable.
status: A 2023 Dirac–Fock/Breit–Gaunt study predicted the oxygen-bound isomer while finding Sg(CO)₆ more stable. An optimized octahedral structure and favorable atomization energy leave kinetic survival unresolved.
why: Tests unusual ligand connectivity at the relativistic edge of coordination chemistry.
key_works: G. L. Malli (2023), “Relativistic and magnetic Breit effects for the reaction Sg + 6CO → Sg(CO)6 and Sg(OC)6: Prediction of the existence and atomization energy of the isomer Sg(OC)6,” [DOI: 10.1063/5.0152081](https://doi.org/10.1063/5.0152081).

title: Complete ligand identities of native nonpertechnetate tank-waste species
open: Assign coordination ligands and molecular structures to low-valent technetium fractions in untreated alkaline tank waste. Quantify transformations introduced by sample processing.
status: AN-102 measurements identified Tc(I) carbonyl and Tc(IV) species in 2020; a 2024 AP-105/AP-107 study added Tc(VI). Positive identification of resin-interacting and unretained species remains incomplete beyond those oxidation-state assignments.
why: Enables treatment of the species escaping pertechnetate-specific capture.
key_works: S. Chatterjee et al. (2020), “Identification and Quantification of Technetium Species in Hanford Waste Tank AN-102,” [DOI: 10.1021/acs.analchem.0c02864](https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.analchem.0c02864); R. M. Asmussen et al. (2024), “The simultaneous removal of technetium and iodine from Hanford tank waste,” [DOI: 10.1016/j.cej.2024.151449](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cej.2024.151449).

title: AmSel selectivity through repeated accumulation of TODGA degradation products
open: Predict and maintain Am/Cm separation through repeated solvent reuse with a changing mixture of TODGA fragments. Measure fragment accumulation and each fragment’s metal-binding contribution.
status: A 2025 study examined individual and combined degradation products and adjustments to stripping conditions. Long-run closure of degradation, regeneration, and selectivity remains a proposed systems extension.
why: Makes extractant radiation resistance meaningful over a process lifetime.
key_works: P. Vacas-Arquero, I. Sánchez-García, and H. Galán (2025), “Influence of the accumulation of TODGA degradation compounds in the separation of Americium from Curium by the AmSel process,” [DOI: 10.1016/j.pnucene.2025.105677](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.pnucene.2025.105677).

title: Predicting methyl-iodide capture by chemically aged silver mordenite
open: Predict breakthrough from measured populations of metallic silver, exchanged Ag(I), and nitrate species after variable NOₓ/moisture histories. Account for iodine capture by each population.
status: A 2020 study identified oxidation and inward silver migration, with nitrates carrying up to 95% of capacity in well-aged samples. A 2024 study adds moisture and storage effects; prospective state-to-breakthrough prediction remains open.
why: Replaces fresh-sorbent capacity assumptions with chemically informed lifetime prediction.
key_works: H. Goettsche et al. (2024), “Effects of moisture and aging upon decomposition of methyl iodide by reduced silver mordenite,” [DOI: 10.1007/s10450-024-00473-8](https://doi.org/10.1007/s10450-024-00473-8); A. I. Wiechert et al. (2020), “Capture of Iodine from Nuclear-Fuel-Reprocessing Off-Gas: Influence of Aging on a Reduced Silver Mordenite Adsorbent after Exposure to NO/NO2,” [DOI: 10.1021/acsami.0c15456](https://doi.org/10.1021/acsami.0c15456).

title: Origin of humidity inhibition in methyl-iodide decomposition on silver mordenite
open: Distinguish water blocking reactant adsorption from product-desorption limitation as the cause of humidity inhibition. If retained products control the rate, identify them and measure their desorption kinetics.
status: The 2024 experiments found approximately 30% slower apparent decomposition under humid conditions. Goettsche’s 2025 dissertation also leaves the rate-limiting step and practical working capacity unresolved because catalytic conversion can obscure iodine retention.
why: Makes disappearance of CH₃I an interpretable measurement of conversion and capture.
key_works: H. Goettsche et al. (2024), “Effects of moisture and aging upon decomposition of methyl iodide by reduced silver mordenite,” [DOI: 10.1007/s10450-024-00473-8](https://doi.org/10.1007/s10450-024-00473-8); H. Goettsche (2025), “Investigations into methyl iodide adsorption and decomposition on reduced silver mordenite,” [doctoral dissertation](https://verso.uidaho.edu/esploro/outputs/doctoral/Investigations-into-methyl-iodide-adsorption-and/996825066201851).

title: The nickel hydride behind additive-switched silylene–Ni hydrosilylation
open: Identify the active Ni species generated by nBuLi from the bis(silylene)-pincer Ni(II) chloride precursor. Determine whether intact pincer-bound Ni–H accounts for Markovnikov selectivity.
status: A 2026 paper reports opposite regioselectivity with nBuLi and KOtBu. It suggests a nickel hydride as the active catalyst under the former conditions without establishing its structure and abundance.
why: Distinguishes ligand-controlled selectivity from additive-induced catalyst reconstruction.
key_works: Z. Yang et al. (2026), “Additive-controlled selective hydrosilylation of aryl alkenes catalyzed by bis(silylene) pincer nickel(II) chloride,” [DOI: 10.1039/D5NJ03998C](https://doi.org/10.1039/D5NJ03998C).

title: Solution-phase N₂ capture by a designed silylene–borole frustrated Lewis pair
open: Synthesize a predicted silylene–borole pair and demonstrate solution-phase N₂ binding and activation. Establish structural identity, reaction rate, and equilibrium constant.
status: The 2025 designs predict barriers of 16.9–22.5 kcal/mol and reaction free energies of −32.3 to −36.7 kcal/mol. N₂ cleavage by SiH₂ in a cryogenic matrix was demonstrated in 2024; the designed solution chemistry remains untested.
why: Tests whether aromaticity-driven cooperativity survives synthesis and solvent effects.
key_works: S. Dong, W. Wang, and J. Zhu (2025), “Design of Borole- and Silylene-Based Frustrated Lewis Pairs for Dinitrogen Activation Promoted by Aromaticity: A Combined DFT and Machine Learning Study,” [DOI: 10.1021/acs.inorgchem.5c02343](https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.inorgchem.5c02343); L. Cai et al. (2024), “N2 cleavage by silylene and formation of H2Si(μ-N)2SiH2,” [DOI: 10.1038/s41467-024-48064-z](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-024-48064-z).

title: A bottleable triplet phosphinidene that avoids intramolecular arene addition
open: Isolate a free, monocoordinate triplet phosphinidene in a hydrindacene-type environment while suppressing reaction with its own aryl framework. Establish its spin state, identity, and solution persistence.
status: The 2024 attempt instead produced singlet phosphanorcaradiene through intramolecular dearomatization. This failed triplet isolation is still discussed in 2026 primary literature; isolated singlet phosphinidenes and precursor equivalents do not fulfill this specific target.
why: Exposes phosphorus-centered triplet chemistry without precursor-release equilibria.
key_works: Y. Chen, P. Su, D. Wang, Z. Ke, and G. Tan (2024), “Molecular-strain induced phosphinidene reactivity of a phosphanorcaradiene,” [DOI: 10.1038/s41467-024-49042-1](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-024-49042-1).

title: The fleeting Sb(III) hydride in disulfide hydroboration
open: Measure the population and lifetime of the proposed hydridostibine between borane metathesis and Sb(I) regeneration. Obtain kinetic evidence discriminating a separately populated hydride from a concerted alternative.
status: The 2024 paper establishes Sb(I)/Sb(III) disulfide-hydroboration turnover and proposes the reaction sequence. Direct hydride-population measurements are a proposed mechanistic test of that account.
why: Tests the elementary event assigned to Sb–H formation and subsequent elimination.
key_works: M. Huang, K. Li, Z. Zhang, and J. Zhou (2024), “Antimony Redox Catalysis: Hydroboration of Disulfides through Unique Sb(I)/Sb(III) Redox Cycling,” [DOI: 10.1021/jacs.4c05905](https://doi.org/10.1021/jacs.4c05905).

title: One-electron versus two-electron flux in antimonate–NHPI aerobic coupling
open: Quantify contributions from Sb-centered single-electron oxidation, PINO-mediated hydrogen abstraction, and the proposed two-electron antimonate pathway. Identify antimony states populated during turnover.
status: The 2013 report explicitly left the roles of antimonate and NHPI unclear. Coupling persisted at 21% yield with a radical inhibitor, motivating an alternative pathway without establishing its structure or flux.
why: Determines whether a catalytic counteranion operates through one mechanism or several.
key_works: A. Tanoue, W.-J. Yoo, and S. Kobayashi (2013), “Antimony/N-Hydroxyphthalimide as a Catalyst System for Cross-Dehydrogenative Coupling Reactions under Aerobic Conditions,” [DOI: 10.1002/adsc.201200999](https://doi.org/10.1002/adsc.201200999).

title: A free phosphatetrazolate [PN₄]⁻ ring
open: Release and isolate aromatic [PN₄]⁻ from its metal coordination environment without nitrogen loss or P–N fragmentation. Determine its counterion dependence and decomposition kinetics.
status: An osmium-bound PN₄ ring was formed in 2025 through phosphorus-mononitride chemistry. Metal-free isolation remains a proposed next target; HCPN₃⁻ and P₂N₃⁻ are different compositions.
why: Tests whether aromatic stabilization sustains this nitrogen-rich phosphorus heterocycle independently.
key_works: S. Edin et al. (2025), “Unleashing phosphorus mononitride,” [DOI: 10.1038/s41467-025-60669-6](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-025-60669-6).

title: The hydridophosphorane in trialkylphosphine-catalysed C–F cleavage
open: Observe hydride transfer to phosphorus and the ensuing hydridophosphorane during pentafluoropyridine hydrodefluorination. Test whether its decay supplies C–H product at the catalytic rate.
status: The 2024 work observes phosphonium intermediates and computationally supports fluorosilicate-mediated hydride delivery followed by reductive elimination. The proposed phosphorus hydride still lacks a direct kinetic assignment during turnover.
why: Tests the central bond-making step of the simple-phosphine redox cycle.
key_works: S. Bonfante, C. Lorber, J. M. Lynam, A. Simonneau, and J. M. Slattery (2024), “Metallomimetic C–F Activation Catalysis by Simple Phosphines,” [DOI: 10.1021/jacs.3c10614](https://doi.org/10.1021/jacs.3c10614).

title: Chloride-versus-sulfate pathway flux in cinnabar blackening
open: Measure contributions of chloride-assisted and sulfate-mediated pathways to HgS conversion into metallic mercury under museum illumination. Close the mercury balance across pigment, binder, secondary salts, and vapor.
status: Metallic mercury was directly demonstrated in photoaged cinnabar tempera in 2021, including a chloride-free pathway. Relative pathway fluxes under ordinary display conditions remain a proposed narrower target.
why: Identifies which environmental intervention slows a particular cinnabar paint.
key_works: K. Elert, M. Pérez Mendoza, and C. Cardell (2021), “Direct evidence for metallic mercury causing photo-induced darkening of red cinnabar tempera paints,” [DOI: 10.1038/s42004-021-00610-2](https://doi.org/10.1038/s42004-021-00610-2).

title: Molecular identity of emerald-green photo-oxidation products
open: Determine stoichiometry, coordination, hydration, and connectivity of the amorphous As(V)-rich products formed during illumination. Distinguish copper arsenates, mixed-cation products, and organically associated arsenate.
status: A 2025 study separated light-driven surface oxidation from humidity-driven arsenolite formation. It explicitly left the structure and stoichiometry of the predominantly amorphous As(V) products unresolved.
why: Product identity determines whether arsenic remains immobilized or migrates.
key_works: S. Carboni Marri et al. (2025), “Discovering the dual degradation pathway of emerald green in oil paints: The effects of light and humidity,” [DOI: 10.1126/sciadv.ady1807](https://doi.org/10.1126/sciadv.ady1807).

title: Sulfur mass balance during orpiment deterioration
open: Quantify sulfur released from deteriorating As₂S₃ as H₂S, dissolved reduced sulfur, oxidized sulfur, and binder-retained species. Link each sulfur pathway to the corresponding arsenic transformation.
status: Broers and colleagues established two arsenic-degradation pathways in 2023 but explicitly excluded sulfur fate from their study. Earlier H₂S suggestions do not establish its yield or competing sinks.
why: Mobile sulfur products can alter neighboring pigments.
key_works: F. T. H. Broers et al. (2023), “Two Pathways for the Degradation of Orpiment Pigment (As2S3) Found in Paintings,” [DOI: 10.1021/jacs.2c12271](https://doi.org/10.1021/jacs.2c12271).

title: Ultramarine sites initiating binder photoradicals
open: Identify the sulfur center, framework defect, or surface state initiating radical damage in ultramarine-containing binders. Connect site assignment to an action spectrum and selective suppression.
status: The 2017 work demonstrated light-induced binder deterioration while pigment remained intact. It established a route to ultramarine disease without assigning the initiating active site.
why: Targeted passivation could preserve both color and binder integrity.
key_works: E. R. de la Rie et al. (2017), “Photo-catalytic degradation of binding media of ultramarine blue containing paint layers: A new perspective on the phenomenon of ‘ultramarine disease’ in paintings,” [DOI: 10.1016/j.polymdegradstab.2017.08.002](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.polymdegradstab.2017.08.002).

title: Water’s catalytic step in zinc-soap crystallization
open: Identify the coordination-changing step through which trace water accelerates zinc-carboxylate crystallization in cured oil. Measure the relevant intermediate, water dependence, and possible catalytic turnover.
status: In 2023, swelling alone did not cause the acceleration, while water-containing solvent induced crystallization. Stabilization of transient charged states was proposed without direct observation of the intermediate.
why: Explains why small water impurities in treatment solvents reorganize metal soaps.
key_works: J. Hermans, K. Helwig, S. Woutersen, and K. Keune (2023), “Traces of water catalyze zinc soap crystallization in solvent-exposed oil paints,” [DOI: 10.1039/D2CP04861B](https://doi.org/10.1039/D2CP04861B).

title: Ambient aluminium catalysis in alum-treated archaeological wood
open: Separate proton-catalyzed damage from aluminium-mediated catalysis at storage temperatures. Identify active aluminium species and quantify their contribution at matched acidity and moisture.
status: Oseberg conservation research and a 2021 collection comparison show that acidity alone does not explain observed damage patterns. Aluminium’s additional ambient catalytic contribution remains insufficiently quantified.
why: Neutralization may leave a degradation pathway active.
key_works: J. J. Łucejko et al. (2021), “Comparative chemical investigations of alum treated archaeological wood from various museum collections,” [publisher article](https://www.nature.com/articles/s40494-021-00517-0); S. Braovac et al. (2018), “Navigating conservation strategies: linking material research on alum-treated wood from the Oseberg collection to conservation decisions,” [DOI: 10.1186/s40494-018-0241-y](https://doi.org/10.1186/s40494-018-0241-y).

title: Native structures of latent copper–sulfhydryl complexes in wine
open: Identify copper complexes storing releasable H₂S, including copper oxidation state, nuclearity, sulfide content, and glutathione coordination. Measure them before analytical reagents perturb their equilibria.
status: Allison and Sacks showed in 2021 that brine release depends on halide chemistry and glutathione. The assay defines a releasable pool without uniquely identifying its native molecular constituents.
why: Predicts whether copper treatment removes sulfur or temporarily conceals it.
key_works: R. B. Allison and G. L. Sacks (2021), “Brine-Releasable Hydrogen Sulfide in Wine: Mechanism of Release from Copper Complexes and Effects of Glutathione,” [DOI: 10.1021/acs.jafc.1c04885](https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.jafc.1c04885).

title: Electron donors sustaining sulfide regeneration in anoxic wine
open: Identify constituents supplying electrons for Cu(II) reduction and conversion of sulfur at oxidation state −I into H₂S sulfur at −II. Balance oxidized organic products against regenerated volatile sulfur.
status: The 2024 remediation study explicitly identifies these electron donors as missing. Copper-treatment, filtration, and adjuvant experiments did not resolve the recurring-sulfide mechanism.
why: Exposes the driver of sulfur recurrence after oxygen depletion.
key_works: D. Sánchez-Gimeno, E. Vela, V. Ferreira, and I. Ontañón (2024), “Alternative strategies for eliminating hydrogen sulfide and methanethiol from wine: results and learnings,” [DOI: 10.20870/oeno-one.2024.58.4.7655](https://doi.org/10.20870/oeno-one.2024.58.4.7655).

title: Non-methionine methanethiol precursors in aged wine
open: Identify the precursor pool sustaining methanethiol production when measured free-methionine depletion cannot account for release. Determine sulfur yields and temperature-dependent conversion kinetics.
status: A 2025 study followed twelve wines for up to eighteen months at 35 °C and shorter periods at higher temperatures. Methanethiol production persisted without closure of the measured precursor balance.
why: Enables prevention of delayed sulfur faults missed by initial volatile measurements.
key_works: S. Ainsa-Zazurca, I. Ontañón, and V. Ferreira (2025), “Kinetic Studies on the Ability of Wines to Produce Hydrogen Sulfide (H2S) and Methanethiol (MeSH),” [DOI: 10.1021/acs.jafc.5c04010](https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.jafc.5c04010).

title: IRC7-independent thiol release in brewing yeast
open: Identify enzymes and substrates responsible for aroma-thiol release retained after IRC7 deletion. Demonstrate necessity and sufficiency using genetic perturbation and enzyme reconstitution.
status: A 2025 comparison found an IRC7 knockout with thiol release resembling its parent. The result implicates alternative routes without identifying the compensating enzyme system.
why: Makes strain performance predictable when the commonly targeted β-lyase gene is insufficient.
key_works: R. Samia, A. Shayevitz, T. Fischborn, and T. H. Shellhammer (2025), “Wort Nitrogen and Yeast Strain Drive Thiol Release, Flavor Expression, and Fermentation Performance in Beer,” [DOI: 10.1080/03610470.2025.2530859](https://doi.org/10.1080/03610470.2025.2530859).

title: Chemical identity of sake fraction DMTS-P2
open: Identify the active constituent or constituents of DMTS-P2 and establish how they yield dimethyl trisulfide. Determine whether activity requires interacting compounds separated during purification.
status: The 2009 work identified DMTS-P1 but left another active fraction unresolved. Isogai’s thesis investigated DMTS-P2 and its interaction with a neutral fraction without converting those operational fractions into molecular structures.
why: Resolves a source of stale-sake sulfur aroma beyond the identified P1 pathway.
key_works: A. Isogai et al. (2009), “Screening and Identification of Precursor Compounds of Dimethyl Trisulfide (DMTS) in Japanese Sake,” [DOI: 10.1021/jf802582p](https://doi.org/10.1021/jf802582p); A. Isogai (2009), “清酒の熟成に関与する香気成分およびその生成機構に関する研究,” [doctoral thesis](https://ir.lib.hiroshima-u.ac.jp/31097/files/19891).

title: Grape-derived dimethyl-trisulfide precursors in wine
open: Identify grape-derived compounds required for substantial DMTS formation during aging. Establish their contribution independently of methanethiol and the sake precursor DMTS-P1.
status: The 2017 study found that dead yeast in synthetic must did not reproduce grape-juice behavior, while known precursors explained only a minor contribution. The operative grape-derived structures remained unidentified.
why: Connects grape and must composition to delayed sulfur defects.
key_works: N. Nishibori, A. Kuroda, O. Yamada, and N. Goto-Yamamoto (2017), “Factors Affecting Dimethyl Trisulfide Formation in Wine,” [DOI: 10.3136/fstr.23.241](https://doi.org/10.3136/fstr.23.241).

title: Chromophore responsible for Sauvignon-blanc pinking
open: Identify the chromophore responsible for the studied Sauvignon-blanc pinking and reproduce its behavior at native concentrations. Distinguish trace anthocyanins from alternative oxidized phenolic products.
status: Anthocyanins were established as a cause in Síria wines in 2014. The 2022 Sauvignon-blanc study remained inconclusive: its 1 mg/L detection limit exceeded the 0.3 mg/L visibility threshold reported for Síria.
why: Improves susceptibility testing and targeted prevention.
key_works: A. P. Nel, W. J. du Toit, and F. P. van Jaarsveld (2022), “Attempted Identification of Causal Constituents of Pink Discolouration in White Wines,” [DOI: 10.21548/43-1-4812](https://doi.org/10.21548/43-1-4812); J. Andrea-Silva et al. (2014), “Origin of the pinking phenomenon of white wines,” [DOI: 10.1021/jf500825h](https://doi.org/10.1021/jf500825h).

title: Fluoride tunneling between two germanium centers of a molecular receptor
open: Realize the proposed double-germanium fluoride receptor and detect low-temperature intersite transfer with a tunneling signature. Distinguish exchange from static disorder and thermal hopping.
status: The ping-pong process was predicted in 2018. The 2025 experimental fluorine-tunneling paper still describes this receptor as hypothetical; its observed polyfluoride system is chemically distinct.
why: Tests deliberate geometric control of tunneling by a relatively heavy nucleus.
key_works: A. Nandi, A. Sucher, and S. Kozuch (2018), “Ping-Pong Tunneling Reactions: Can Fluoride Jump at Absolute Zero?” [DOI: 10.1002/chem.201802782](https://doi.org/10.1002/chem.201802782); C. Müller et al. (2025), “Experimental observation of quantum mechanical fluorine tunnelling,” [DOI: 10.1038/s41467-025-59008-6](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-025-59008-6).

title: Experimental verification of tunneling-driven XeF₆ pseudorotation
open: Separate quantum tunneling from residual thermal motion in low-temperature XeF₆ pseudorotation. Identify predicted splittings or isotope-sensitive exchange in a characterized environment.
status: Sedgi and Kozuch predicted rapid near-zero-temperature fluorine tunneling in 2020. The 2025 polyfluoride study still cites XeF₆ as a computational prediction.
why: Tests quantum dynamics in a classic fluxional hypervalent molecule.
key_works: I. Sedgi and S. Kozuch (2020), “Heavy atom tunnelling on XeF6 pseudorotation,” [DOI: 10.1039/D0CP03205K](https://doi.org/10.1039/D0CP03205K); C. Müller et al. (2025), “Experimental observation of quantum mechanical fluorine tunnelling,” [DOI: 10.1038/s41467-025-59008-6](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-025-59008-6).

title: Testing hyperconjugation as the cause of solvent-enhanced carbon tunneling
open: Test whether coordination-dependent geminal hyperconjugation explains tunneling-rate changes in the benzene oxide/oxepin system. Independently constrain coordination populations and distinguish barrier narrowing from energetic stabilization.
status: The 2025 calculations connect coordination motifs to C–C shortening and enhanced tunneling. Solvent-controlled tunneling already has experimental precedents; the open target is this proposed electronic cause and its quantitative prediction.
why: Could make solvent selection a rational control of heavy-atom tunneling.
key_works: C. J. Laconsay, I. Jain, T. Schleif, W. L. Karney, and J. I. Wu (2025), “Geminal hyperconjugation as a driving force for C–C bond shortening in heavy-atom tunnelling,” [DOI: 10.1039/D5SC02914G](https://doi.org/10.1039/D5SC02914G).

title: General sequencing of branched native glycans
open: Determine monosaccharide identity, linkage position, anomeric configuration and branching for arbitrary glycans in mixtures, with calibrated structural ambiguity.
status: A longstanding structural problem. Enzymatic nanopore decoding in 2025 and fragment reassembly in 2026 established partial routes; universal sequencing remains open.
why: Enables complete characterization of glycoproteins and cell-surface recognition chemistry.
key_works: Xia et al. (2026), *Nanopore-Based Glycan Sequencing via a Fragmentation-Reassembly Strategy*, [DOI:10.1021/jacs.5c22760](https://doi.org/10.1021/jacs.5c22760).

title: Individually addressable carborane vertices
open: Functionalize any chosen non-equivalent boron vertex of a carborane cage, including sequential different substitutions, with controlled cage and substituent stereochemistry.
status: A longstanding cluster-synthesis problem. A 2025 rhodium-carbene method achieved site- and enantioselective B–H insertion for selected carboranes; complete vertex addressability remains unavailable.
why: Expands three-dimensional pharmacophores, ligands and electronically unusual materials.
key_works: Lee et al. (2025), *Site- and enantioselective B−H functionalization of carboranes*, [DOI:10.1038/s41467-025-59410-0](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-025-59410-0).

title: Molecular parity-violating enantiomer energy difference
open: Measure the electroweak energy or transition-frequency difference between molecular enantiomers with systematic errors below the predicted signal.
status: Predicted for decades. A July 2026 proposal still describes molecular parity violation as experimentally undetected; heavy chiral species and ultracold amplification provide possible routes.
why: It would test the weak interaction in molecular matter and constrain microscopic sources of chiral bias.
key_works: D. Martínez-Gil, P. Bargueño and S. Miret-Artés (2026), *Ultracold amplification proposal for parity violation in chiral molecules*, [DOI:10.1103/54yp-6397](https://doi.org/10.1103/54yp-6397); [arXiv:2606.08717](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.08717).

title: Indefinite nonenzymatic RNA replication
open: Couple copying, strand separation and substrate replenishment into repeated enzyme-free replication of mixed-sequence RNA without externally resetting each generation.
status: Chemical copying has advanced for decades. Virtual-circular-genome experiments in 2023 tested a route around duplex trapping without establishing indefinite autonomous replication.
why: Bridges prebiotic synthesis and Darwinian heredity.
key_works: Ding et al. (2023), *Experimental Tests of the Virtual Circular Genome Model for Nonenzymatic RNA Replication*, [DOI:10.1021/jacs.3c00612](https://doi.org/10.1021/jacs.3c00612).

title: Carrier and charge state of the 8621 Å diffuse interstellar band
open: Assign the 862.1 nm band to a molecule and charge state using laboratory spectra and a consistent photoionization/recombination model.
status: A 2026 study of 12 clouds finds spatial behavior supporting a cation. Ionization-energy constraints remain model-dependent and do not identify the molecule.
why: Gives Gaia’s extensive DIB measurements a chemical identity.
key_works: H. Zhao and L. Li (2026), *A cationic carrier for the diffuse interstellar band at 862.1 nm: Evidence of the skin effect in nearby diffuse to translucent clouds*, [DOI:10.1051/0004-6361/202557833](https://doi.org/10.1051/0004-6361/202557833); [arXiv:2603.05631](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.05631).

title: Substrate-oxygen assignment in photosystem II
open: Determine experimentally which two oxygen atoms form O₂, distinguishing O5–O6 coupling from the competing O3–O6 proposal.
status: A 2026 calculation proposed O3–O6 coupling, while new structural measurements located the additional S₃-state oxygen without directly identifying the reacting pair. The remaining target is an experimentally discriminating atom assignment.

title: Proton-and-electron-only recycling of triphenylphosphine oxide
open: Reduce ordinary triphenylphosphine oxide to triphenylphosphine using electricity and a proton source, without stoichiometric silanes, hydrides, or halogenating activators.
status: A 2026 study achieved 90% yield for a specially designed fused dipyridyl phosphine oxide; extending this proton-coupled reduction to commodity phosphine oxides remains open.
why: Could close phosphorus-reagent cycles in widely used organic reactions.
key_works: A. Laverny et al. (2026), *Proton-coupled electrochemical reduction of a phosphine oxide*, [DOI:10.1016/j.chempr.2026.102946](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.chempr.2026.102946).

title: Causal product control by the initial electronic coherence
open: Demonstrate that changing an initial electronic relative phase, at fixed populations and deposited energy, changes a later product distribution.
status: Full-dimensional ethylene simulations in 2025 predict altered nuclear motion despite rapid electronic decoherence. The controlled experimental phase-to-product test remains open.
why: Establishes whether attosecond coherent control can deliver chemical selectivity.
key_works: L. Fransén et al. (2025), *Attochemical Control of Nuclear Motion despite Fast Electronic Decoherence*, [DOI:10.1021/acs.jpclett.5c01895](https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.jpclett.5c01895).

title: Equimolar oxidative cross-Kolbe coupling
open: Selectively couple two different free aliphatic carboxylic acids at approximately equimolar loading by oxidative decarboxylation, without converting either into an activated ester.
status: Reductive heterocoupling through activated esters is established. The 2023 waveform-controlled oxidative method broadened direct scope without establishing general nonstatistical cross-coupling of similar acids.
why: Makes abundant acids interchangeable coupling partners with less activation waste.
key_works: B. Zhang et al. (2022), *Ni-electrocatalytic Csp3–Csp3 doubly decarboxylative coupling*, [DOI:10.1038/s41586-022-04691-4](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-022-04691-4); Y. Hioki et al. (2023), *Overcoming the limitations of Kolbe coupling with waveform-controlled electrosynthesis*, [DOI:10.1126/science.adf4762](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.adf4762).

title: Address-selective hydrocarboxylation of internal alkenes
open: Add CO₂ and hydrogen across either chosen carbon of an unactivated internal alkene while retaining the original double-bond position as the reaction site.
status: Alternating-polarity hydrocarboxylation and migratory carboxylation advanced in 2025–2026. Those methods leave independently selectable, nonmigratory internal-alkene regiochemistry unresolved.
why: Converts inexpensive internal olefins into specific acid building blocks.
key_works: Fors, Yap and Malapit (2025), *Effect of Alternating Polarity in Electrochemical Olefin Hydrocarboxylation*, [DOI:10.1002/anie.202424865](https://doi.org/10.1002/anie.202424865); M. Dong et al. (2026), *Electrocatalytic Migratory Carboxylation of Unactivated Olefins or Halides with CO2*, [DOI:10.1002/anie.202518160](https://doi.org/10.1002/anie.202518160).

title: Localizing three or more adjacent mucin O-glycans
open: Assign individual glycan compositions to three or more nearby serine/threonine residues with calibrated confidence, separating isomers having identical total composition.
status: The 2026 DeepGPO framework supports singly and doubly glycosylated peptides. Its authors identify three-plus glycans as beyond current capability because of spectral complexity and scarce training data.
why: Resolves dense site patterns defining mucin surfaces.
key_works: Y. Zong, Y. Wang and L. Qiao (2026), *Deep Learning Prediction of O-Glycopeptide Tandem Mass Spectra Enhances O-Glycoproteomics*, [DOI:10.1002/advs.76760](https://doi.org/10.1002/advs.76760).

title: Complete intact-ganglioside structural assignment
open: Determine glycan sequence and linkage, ceramide chains, every double-bond position and relevant stereochemistry on the same native molecule.
status: A 2026 HILIC–nanoESI-MS/MS workflow quantified 80 species across 18 subclasses in ten mouse tissues. Molecular-species annotation still falls short of complete stereochemical structures.
why: Distinguishes compositionally identical molecules with different membrane functions.
key_works: N. Troppmair et al. (2026), *Comprehensive Isomer-Resolved Ganglioside Profiling by HILIC-nanoESI-MS/MS*, [DOI:10.1021/acs.analchem.6c00380](https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.analchem.6c00380).

title: Secure detection of interstellar glycine
open: Identify interstellar glycine through multiple unblended transitions with consistent excitation and abundance, no missing strong lines and explicit conformer discrimination.
status: The disputed early-2000s claim never became secure. A September 2026 preprint still treats interstellar glycine as undetected and examines conformer kinetics as a search constraint.
why: Anchors links between interstellar chemistry and planetary amino-acid inventories.
key_works: L. E. Snyder et al. (2005), *A Rigorous Attempt to Verify Interstellar Glycine*, [NIST record](https://www.nist.gov/publications/rigorous-attempt-verify-interstellar-glycine); J. Wurmel and J. M. Simmie (2026), *Glycine in the interstellar medium revisited: Resolving conformational complexity kinetically*, [arXiv:2609.17243](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.17243).

title: Motif-II structure of the hydrated electron in water clusters
open: Assign the atomic structure and electron-binding geometry of motif II in size-selected water-cluster anions. A convincing assignment must explain photoelectron and absorption measurements obtained under the same source conditions.
status: An and Kim’s 2026 measurements expanded the experimentally distinguished motifs from four to five; the correspondence between motif II and calculated structures remains unresolved.
why: A secure assignment would test how a small hydrogen-bond network stabilizes an excess electron.
key_works: S. An and S. K. Kim (2026), “Structure and isomer-specific femtosecond real-time relaxation dynamics of hydrated electron motifs in water cluster anions,” [DOI: 10.1038/s42004-026-02006-6](https://doi.org/10.1038/s42004-026-02006-6).

title: Water evaporation versus electron loss in the 340-ps cluster-anion decay
open: Resolve the branching between neutral-water evaporation and electron autodetachment from vibrationally excited water-cluster anions, including its dependence on cluster size and electron-binding motif.
status: An and Kim (2026) observed an approximately 340-ps ground-state decay component and provisionally attributed it to evaporation and/or autodetachment; channel-specific identification remains open.
why: Establishes how small hydrated electrons survive after optical excitation.
key_works: S. An and S. K. Kim (2026), “Structure and isomer-specific femtosecond real-time relaxation dynamics of hydrated electron motifs in water cluster anions,” [DOI: 10.1038/s42004-026-02006-6](https://doi.org/10.1038/s42004-026-02006-6).

title: Unknown side products that divert irradiated chromium recombination
open: Identify the accumulating products that cause Cr(I)/Cr(III) recombination in molten LiCl–KCl to depart from second-order kinetics, and determine their reaction pathways.
status: Pulse-radiolysis measurements resolved primary reactions, but increasing accumulated dose introduced competing chemistry whose products remained unidentified.
why: Reveals when reversible radiation chemistry produces persistent changes in a molten salt.
key_works: K. Iwamatsu et al. (2026; first published 2025), “Kinetics of radiation-induced Cr(II) and Cr(III) redox chemistry in molten LiCl–KCl eutectic,” [DOI: 10.1039/D4CP04190A](https://doi.org/10.1039/D4CP04190A).

title: Room-temperature Pr(V) persistence beyond the demonstrated protective ligand environment
open: Isolate a room-temperature-persistent molecular Pr(V) complex beyond the demonstrated heavily shielded imidophosphorane environment. Measure decomposition kinetics and establish its electronic-state assignment.
status: Molecular formal Pr(V) was isolated at low temperature in 2025. A 2026 ligand comparison found modest redox-potential changes but major stability differences, with some Pr(V) states observable only electrochemically.
why: Enables systematic high-valent lanthanide reactivity beyond specially protected examples.
key_works: A. C. Boggiano et al. (2025), “Praseodymium in the formal +5 oxidation state,” [DOI: 10.1038/s41557-025-01797-w](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41557-025-01797-w); T.-R. Nero et al. (2026), “Ligand Design Criteria for the Stability of High Oxidation State Praseodymium Complexes,” [DOI: 10.1021/acs.inorgchem.5c05024](https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.inorgchem.5c05024).

title: High-turnover elemental-germanium bromoalkylation with a closed inventory
open: Develop mechanically activated elemental Ge for alkene bromoalkylation with measured recovery and losses. A proposed engineering milestone is at least 100 cumulative turnovers without continuous net consumption of the Ge inventory.
status: Guo and colleagues demonstrated activation and catalytic bromoalkylation in 2025, alongside separate Ge recycling experiments. The 100-turnover criterion with a complete inventory is a proposed assessment, not a reported record.
why: Establishes whether elemental Ge can function as a reusable process material.
key_works: G. Guo et al. (2025), “Elemental Germanium Activation and Catalysis Enabled by Mechanical Force,” [DOI: 10.1002/anie.202421446](https://doi.org/10.1002/anie.202421446).

title: The transient silane–silylium ion in stibenium-catalysed Si–C redistribution
open: Detect or kinetically discriminate the proposed [Et₂HSi···H–SiEt₃]⁺ intermediate during constrained-stibenium silane redistribution. Establish whether it carries exchange between Et₃SiH and Et₂SiH₂/Et₄Si.
status: The 2026 work demonstrates Si–C activation and identifies Sb(V) species supporting the cycle. The short-lived silane–silylium carrier remains proposed.
why: Distinguishes antimony-centered exchange from cationic silicon propagation.
key_works: D. Toami and R. Dobrovetsky (2026), “Structurally Constrained Stibenium: Metallomimetic C−Si Bond Activation,” [DOI: 10.1002/anie.3059944](https://doi.org/10.1002/anie.3059944).

title: An isolable molecular antimony-mononitride adduct
open: Stabilize an intact SbN unit in an isolable molecular adduct. Establish its bonding and isotope-sensitive vibrational signature.
status: Gas-phase SbN spectroscopy dates to Coy and Sponer’s 1940 experiments. Qian and colleagues’ 2026 primary comparison lists SbN as detected but not isolated.
why: Isolable samples would test how coordination stabilizes a heavy-element nitride.
key_works: N. H. Coy and H. Sponer (1940), “Emission Spectrum of Antimony Nitride,” [DOI: 10.1103/PhysRev.58.709](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRev.58.709); W. Qian et al. (2026), “Synthesis of an o-Benzoquinone Arsenic Mononitride (As≡N) Complex and Its Reaction to Singlet Arsinonitrene,” [DOI: 10.1021/jacs.5c20377](https://doi.org/10.1021/jacs.5c20377).

title: Carbon and electron sources of iron oxalate in gall-ink paper
open: Determine whether oxalate in aged gall-ink paper derives from cellulose, ink polyphenols, or another component. Identify the coupled electron donor for Fe(III) reduction.
status: A 2026 ink/mockup study observed ferrous oxalate emerging as ferric polyphenol complexes were depleted. Product detection did not establish its carbon source or complete redox balance.
why: Determines whether iron oxalate diagnoses paper destruction, ink alteration, or both.
key_works: M. Nunes et al. (2026), “From Ink to Mockup: An Integrated Study of Historical Gall Ink Formulations and Their Impact on Paper,” [DOI: 10.1002/cplu.202500369](https://doi.org/10.1002/cplu.202500369).

title: The simultaneous DOE ultimate PEM electrolyser target
subfield: Water splitting, hydrogen production and fuel cells
open: Meet the official ultimate targets on one practical stack: 3 A cm⁻² at 1.6 V per cell, 0.125 mg cm⁻² total platinum-group metals and 80,000-hour lifetime, alongside cost requirements.
status: This is a combined target. A 2025 study achieved below 1.75 V at 4 A cm⁻² with 0.375 mg Ir cm⁻², advancing only some constraints.
why: It would reduce renewable hydrogen’s material and capital intensity.
